title: In vivo proteolytic profiling of the type I and type II metacaspases in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii exposed to salt stress
projectDescription: Metacaspases are cysteine proteases present in plants, fungi and protists. While the association of metacaspases with cell death is studied in a range of organisms, their native substrates are largely unknown. Here, we explored the in vivo proteolytic landscape of the two metacaspases, CrMCA-I and CrMCA-II, present in the green freshwater alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, using N-terminal peptide labelling and enrichment during standard conditions and salt stress. Comparison between the cleavage events of CrMCA-I and CrMCA-II in metacaspase mutants revealed unique cleavage preferences and substrate specificity. Degradome analysis demonstrated relevance of the predicted metacaspase substrates to the physiology of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii cells and its adaptation during salt stress. Functional enrichment analysis indicated an involvement of CrMCA-I in photosynthesis and translation, while CrMCA-II seems to be important during the catabolism of carboxylic acids. Altogether, our findings suggest distinct cellular functions of the two metacaspases in C. reinhardtii during salt stress response.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Four experimental groups were prepared: WT vs. mcaI and WT vs. mcaII grown in control conditions and WT vs. mcaI and WT vs. mcaII grown in salt stress. For every WT and mutant sample, treated and untreated, three biological replicates were pooled. 50 mL of liquid culture (containing 0.8 - 1x108 mL-1 cells) of WT and mutant strains, were harvested by centrifugation at 1610 x g for 3 min. The biomass was frozen in liquid nitrogen and broken down into a fine powder with mortar and pestle. The material was dissolved in 0.5 ml ice-cold lysis buffer composed of Hepes, pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.4% NP-40 (w/v) in water, a protease inhibitor cocktail tablet (Roche, cat. no. 11697498001), 2 mM DTT, and 0.4% Amphipol A8-35 (w/v) and incubated on ice for 30 minutes. Cell lysis was further promoted with 3 cycles of freeze-thawing and 4-fold dilution with 25mM Hepes pH7.5, 25mM NaCl) and 3 rounds of point sonication, followed by centrifugation at 16,000g for 30 min at 4°C. Proteins were denatured and S-alkylated followed by Amphipol precipitation. The supernatans were discarded and pellets were resuspended in Tri-ethyl Ammonium bicarbonate buffer. All α- and ɛ-amines (protein N-terminus and lysine residues) were butylated with an N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) ester of light 12C4-butyrate (WT) or heavy 13C4-butyrate (leg -/-). After Amphipol precipitation and resuspension in TEAB buffer, WT and knock-out mutants were mixed 1:1  followed by trypsin digestion (cleaving only after arginine residues since lysine residues are blocked). Then, in the resulting 4 samples, N-terminally blocked peptides were enriched by Strong Cation Exchange (SCX) at pH3, as such peptides will not bind to the SCX resin at low pH. N-terminal glutamine is able to form a cyclic ring which results in a peptide with a net charge of zero (at the pH used), similar to the blocked N-terminal peptides. To prevent this, pyroglutamate removal was performed prior to the actual SCX step. Finally, to reduce sample complexity resulting from incomplete oxidations on methionine residues during sample handling, all methionine residues were oxidized with hydrogen peroxide followed by peptide purification using Omix purification tips (C18 reversed phase).  Finally, 5 µl of this solution was injected for LC-MS/MS analysis. LC-MS/MS was performed on an Ultimate 3000 RSLC nano liquid chromatography system (Thermo) in line connected to a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo, Germany). Trapping was performed at 10 μl min-1 for 4 min in loading solvent A on a 20 mm trapping column (made in-house, 100 μm internal diameter (I.D.), 5 μm beads, C18 Reprosil-HD, Dr. Maisch, Germany). The peptides were separated on a nanoEase column (MZ HSS T3 1.8 μm, 75 μm x 250 mm, Waters, part: 186008818)) kept at a constant temperature of 50°C. Peptides were eluted by a non-linear gradient reaching 33% MS solvent B (0.1% FA in water/acetonitrile (2:8, v/v)) in 147 min, 55% MS solvent B in 203 min and 99% MS solvent B  in 210 min at a constant flow rate of 300 nl min-1, followed by a 10-minutes wash at 99% MS solvent B and re-equilibration with MS solvent A (0.1% FA in water). The mass spectrometer was operated in data-dependent mode, automatically switching between MS and MS/MS acquisition for the 8 most abundant ion peaks per MS spectrum. Full-scan MS spectra (375-1,500 m/z) were acquired at a resolution of 60,000 in the Orbitrap analyzer after accumulation to a target value of 3,000,000. The 8 most intense ions above a threshold value of 10,000 (minimum AGC of 1,000) were isolated for fragmentation at a normalized collision energy of 28%. The C-trap was filled at a target value of 100,000 for maximum 100 ms and the MS/MS spectra (200-2,000 m/z) were acquired at a resolution of 15,000 in the Orbitrap analyzer with a fixed first mass of 145 m/z. Only peptides with charges between +2 and +6 were included for fragmentation and the dynamic exclusion was set to 45 s.
dataProcessingProtocol: Recorded spectra of all 4 groups were searched separately to identify peptides and proteins using the Mascot algorithm (version 2.8.2, https://www.matrixscience.com/). Spectrum matching was performed against the C. reinhardtii protein sequences in the Swiss-Prot reference proteome (database release version of 2020_06, UP000006906, 18,829 protein entries downloaded from www.uniprot.org). In this search, N-terminal butylation was set as a fixed modification using a quantitation method, where peptides containing light butylation (+0 Da) on α- and ɛ-amines were configured as light component, while peptides containing heavy butylation (+4 Da) on α- and ɛ-amines were configured as heavy component. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues and oxidation of methionine residues were set as fixed modifications. In a second parallel search the cyclisation of N-terminal glutamine residues and acetylation of protein N-termini (due to in vivo acetylation) were set as variable modifications to also identify peptides that were not labelled by butylation on their N-terminus. In this search, butylation of lysine residues was set as a fixed modification using a quantitation method, where peptides containing the butylation labels (+0 Da or +4 Da) only on the α- amines were configured as light or heavy component. Carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues and oxidation of methionine residues were again set as fixed modifications.  From both searches peptide identifications exceeding the Mascot identity threshold score at 99% significance were parsed and stored in the in-house ms_lims database (Helsens et al. 2010). This step includes selecting only for the best scoring match for each spectrum with a positive hit in both the searches. All identified peptides were quantified by the Mascot Distiller quantitation algorithm (version 2.7.1.0, https://www.matrixscience.com/). In parallel, all peptides identified with a butylated N-terminus not starting at position 1 or 2, comprising potential cleavage sites, were additionally quantified by the Skyline software, which reported several quantitation quality measures including the rdotp, idotp and ppm deviation values. In a next step, quantitation outputs from Mascot Distiller and Skyline were integrated automatically using a KNIME workflow to generate a list of potential single (or near single) light labelled neo-N-termini. This list was further manually validated and curated using Skyline to come to a final list of high- and low-quality neo-N-terminal peptides. High-quality peptides are characterized by an intense MS1 signal and complete absence of a heavy isotopic envelope. Low-quality peptides showed a lower MS1 intensity, a remaining heavy isotopic envelope (normalized log2 L/H ratio >2.32) and/or noise peaks at the expected position of the heavy envelope.
